Functionality (round-trip, atomicity, cleanup on serialization/replace failure) is correct and all 4 tests pass. However there's a real regression: `tempfile.mkstemp` creates the temp file with mode 0600, and since `os.replace()` moves that inode into place, the saved file ends up with 0600 permissions instead of the umask-respecting default (typically 0644) that the original `open(path, 'w')` produced.

Verified directly:
```
os.umask(0o022)
app.save(p, {'a': 1})
oct(stat.S_IMODE(os.stat(p).st_mode))  # -> '0o600'  (was 0o644 before the change)
```

This also silently downgrades permissions on pre-existing destination files when overwritten (os.replace() takes on the source file's mode, discarding whatever mode the destination previously had). The task says to preserve existing behavior except where explicitly changed, and file permissions were not part of the requested change, so this is an unintended regression.

Fix: after `os.fdopen`/writing, `os.chmod(tmp_path, 0o666 & ~os.umask(0)) ` (restoring the umask immediately after reading it) before the `os.replace`, or otherwise ensure the temp file's mode matches what `open(path, 'w')` would have produced. No test currently covers file permissions — worth adding one.

Tests pass (5/5) and the previously-flagged issue (new files getting mkstemp's restrictive 0600 instead of the umask-default mode) is now correctly fixed and covered by a test.

However, there's a related regression that's still unaddressed: when **overwriting an existing file**, the new file's permissions are reset to the umask-default instead of preserving the existing destination's mode. The original `open(path, 'w')` truncates in place, so a pre-existing file's custom permissions (e.g. 0600 on a secrets/credentials JSON file) were preserved across saves. The new atomic implementation always swaps in a new inode via `os.replace()`, so the destination's prior mode is discarded and replaced with whatever mode the temp file has (now umask-default, e.g. 0644) — silently loosening permissions on files that were deliberately locked down.

Reproduced directly:
```python
app.save(p, {'a': 1})
os.chmod(p, 0o600)          # e.g. a secrets file
print(oct(os.stat(p).st_mode))   # 0o600
app.save(p, {'a': 2})       # normal overwrite, umask 022
print(oct(os.stat(p).st_mode))   # 0o644  <- destination's original mode lost
```

This is the same category of "preserve existing behavior" issue flagged previously, just the overwrite case rather than the create case. Fix: before writing, if the destination path already exists, `os.chmod(tmp_path, stat.S_IMODE(os.stat(path).st_mode))` to match it (falling back to the current umask-based default when the destination doesn't exist yet). No test currently covers overwrite-permission preservation — worth adding one alongside the fix.

This is an extremely low-probability edge case not covered by the task's explicit failure scenarios (serialization/replacement failure) and isn't blocking.

Concrete bug found: app.py splits the input with `text.splitlines()`, which treats several Unicode characters beyond `\n`/`\r\n` as line breaks — specifically `\x85` (NEL), ` ` (LINE SEPARATOR), and ` ` (PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR). These are legal, unescaped characters inside a JSON string (JSON only requires escaping control chars U+0000–U+001F, `"`, and `\`), so a fully valid JSONL line whose `title` contains a raw ` ` gets split mid-object into two garbage fragments. Both fragments are then rejected, and every subsequent line's physical line number is thrown off by one.

Repro:
```python
from app import parse_jsonl
text = '{"id":1,"title":"a b"}\n{"id":2,"title":"c"}'
records, errors = parse_jsonl(text)
# records == [{'id': 2, 'title': 'c'}]   (record 1, which is valid, is lost)
# errors  == [1, 2]                       (should be [], both lines are valid)
```

Fix: split on `\n` only (e.g. `text.split("\n")`, stripping a trailing `\r` per line for CRLF support) instead of `str.splitlines()`, so "physical line" matches the conventional definition and doesn't over-split on characters that are legal inside JSON string values.

Verified fix: app.py now splits with text.split("\n") (stripping trailing \r), so Unicode line separators ( ,  , \x85) inside JSON string values no longer fragment a valid record. Reran the original repro — both records now parse correctly with no errors. All 15 tests pass. No other correctness issues found (duplicate-ID handling, id/title validation, error line numbering, continuation after bad lines all verified correct).
